episodes.211834: A weak disturbance moving across the Intermountain West combined with intense daytime heating resulting in scattered high based evaporating showers and dry thunderstorms across western and central New Mexico during the afternoon hours on May 13th. These showers resulted in dry microbursts at the Farmington Four Corners Regional Airport and the NMDOT weather station along I-40 at SR6 in Laguna Pueblo. High based shower and thunderstorm activity across western and central New Mexico dissipated around sunset with the loss of daytime heating. Two rounds of high based shower and thunderstorm activity developed across the eastern plains of New Mexico during the afternoon hours on May 14th and 15th with dry microbursts in Clayton. High based shower and thunderstorm activity exited east into west Texas and tapered off during the evening hours, with one area of collapsing showers resulting in a heat burst at the Fort Sumner Municipal Airport late on May 14th.
episodes.211888: A shortwave embedded in the flow aloft neared the area on the 14th. Meanwhile, mid-to-upper level moisture moved over the region. Lift from the shortwave interacted with this moisture and allowed isolated to scattered high-based showers and storms to develop across the area. Low-levels were very dry, so most rain evaporated before it hit the ground. Because of this evaporative cooling, a few showers and storms managed to produce severe downbursts. Convection largely diminished after dark.
episodes.211889: The synoptic setup was similar to May 14th, with a nearby shortwave interacting with elevated moisture to produce a few high-based thunderstorms (mainly over southeast New Mexico and the Permian Basin). A couple of thunderstorms managed to produce damaging downburst winds, including an 84 mph gust in northern Gaines County. Convection largely diminished after dark.
episodes.211890: The synoptic setup was similar to May 14th, with a nearby shortwave interacting with elevated moisture to produce a few high-based thunderstorms (mainly over southeast New Mexico and the Permian Basin). A couple of thunderstorms managed to produce damaging downburst winds, including an 84 mph gust in northern Gaines County. Convection largely diminished after dark.
episodes.211918: A cold upper level low approached the Hawaiian islands and led to thunderstorms and flooding.
episodes.211983: Very hot temperatures on the afternoon of the 14th combined with mid-level moisture to create numerous high-based thunderstorms. The lowest levels of the atmosphere were very dry which allowed for most of the rainfall to evaporate before reaching the surface. The rapidly sinking air near thunderstorms resulted in strong to severe gusts upon impacting the ground. The intense winds also kicked up copious amounts of dust creating brief brownouts in localized areas. Furthermore, dry lightning initiated a wildfire just west of Matador. This wildfire was named the Crooked Cook Fire and burned approximately 1388 acres before being contained on the 15th. No known damage occurred from this wildfire.
episodes.211987: The afternoon of the 15th saw a repeat of the previous day's activity. Very hot temperatures on the afternoon of the 15th combined with mid-level moisture to create numerous high-based thunderstorms. The lowest levels of the atmosphere were very dry which allowed for most of the rainfall to evaporate before reaching the surface. The rapidly sinking air near thunderstorms resulted in strong to severe gusts upon impacting the ground. The intense winds also kicked up copious amounts of dust creating brief brownouts in localized areas. Several wildfire starts occurred on the afternoon of the 15th although none of these wildfires caused any known damage. The Cherokee Fire within the canyon of Briscoe County burned a total of approximately 3,222 acres. The Ox Bow Fire started in rural Hall County northeast of Turkey burned approximately 1,000 acres before being contained on the 16th. The Chainey Mountain Fire also started in Hall County near the Childress County line and burned approximately 1,200 acres before being contained on the 16th. The Baylor Creek Fire started just northeast of the Chainey Mountain Fire and burned 195 acres crossing the Hall/Childress County line. The last known wildfire for the day began in Motley County called the Comanche Fire. This wildfire burned approximately 1,991 acres before being contained on the 17th.
episodes.212651: A small cluster of thunderstorms moved across Harper and Kingman counties during the evening hours of May 14th. Winds were reported to be 60 mph near Anthony, and wind damage was reported near Norwich.
episodes.212805: A couple low-precipitation supercells moved across portions of north-central Kansas on the evening of May 14, with sporadic strong winds and large hail.
episodes.213066: Thunderstorms brought large hail and damaging wind gusts to eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa during the late afternoon and evening hours of May 15, 2026. Through the afternoon, moisture pooled along a surface front, with an upper-level shortwave initiating convective development. Surface-based instability (SBCAPE) of 2000 to 2500 J/kg materialized across the region. This instability, combined with 35 to 40 knots of deep-layer (0-6 km) bulk shear, initially favored discrete supercell development. Atmospheric soundings revealed fairly dry low levels, which enhanced the threat for severe, damaging wind gusts as the convection transitioned into an outflow-dominated regime. Additional storms developed along the boundary across far eastern Nebraska into the evening hours before the entire line eventually became outflow-dominant and weakened.||Several notable severe weather impacts were reported across southwest Iowa and eastern Nebraska during the event, primarily driven by damaging wind gusts and hail. The most significant wind damage occurred in southwest Iowa, where gusts estimated between 60 and 75 mph caused structural and agricultural damage. A measured gust of 74 mph was recorded by the Red Oak, IA AWOS, which correlated with amateur radio reports of downed power poles, tree damage, and widespread power outages in the city. In Mills County, severe winds blew over farm augers and moved grain wagons near Randolph, while structural damage to roofing and siding was reported further east in Stanton. Alongside the wind threat, severe hail up to 1.00 inch in diameter (quarter-sized) was widely reported across the region, including instances in Cass, Seward, Washington, and Douglas counties in Nebraska���with one 1.00-inch hail report coming directly from an NWS employee in Valley, NE.

episodes.213369: High-based showers and thunderstorms produced dry microbursts and several observations of severe wind gusts across western Oklahoma on the evening of the 15th.
episodes.213879: An upper level low and surface front produced strong winds across northern North Dakota. There were a few isolated thunderstorms early in the day before non-thunderstorm wind gusts reached around 60 mph. The highest observed non-thunderstorm wind gust was 62 mph in Rolette.
episodes.213967: The primary breakup front from the Upper Yukon tracked down through the middle section of the Yukon during the middle part of May. While some snowmelt flooding remained over parts of the Upper Yukon, primary dynamics shifted to significant mechanical ice jam releases, notably near the mouth of the Yuki River jam, which caused rapid surges downstream.
episodes.214233: On May 15, 2026, a widespread soaking rainfall event delivered heavy precipitation across the White Mountains region, producing basin-wide averages of 2.75 inches in the Pemigewasset Basin and approximately 3.25 inches in the Upper Saco Basin. Rapid runoff from the heavy rain caused river levels to rise quickly above flood stage in both New Hampshire. The resulting minor flooding inundated low-lying areas and riverside campgrounds in Grafton and Carroll Counties. While no structural damage was reported, the sudden rise in water levels disrupted early-season recreational activity before both rivers receded back into their banks.
episodes.214298: The right entrance region of a jet within stronger flow across the northern tier of the U.S. helped to increase convergence by late afternoon and early evening along a cold front working eastward through northwest Iowa.  Mixed-layer instability reached up to 1500-2000 J/kg courtesy of 8C/km mid-level lapse rates with deep-layer shear of 40 to 50 knots. Initially discrete cells produced large hail, with a tendency to evolve toward more linear structures.

A Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet site near Graham measured severe wind gusts of 58 mph from 1848 CST to 1849 CST.
The West Texas Mesonet station 15 Seagraves 1SW measured a 59 mph wind gust associated with a  convective downburst.

An ice jam near the mouth of the Yuki River released a massive surge of water. As this front surged past Galena and Koyukuk, the Galena river gauge recorded a minor flood crest of 124.8 feet on May 15, before slowly receding into action stage (123.7 feet) by May 17.
A NASA Davis Vantage Pro 2 weather station at Fort Sumner Municipal Airport measured a brief 67 mph wind gust due to a heat burst caused by nearby collapsing showers.

Heavy rainfall on May 15 brought basin-average precipitation of 3.25 inches to the Upper Saco Basin. The resulting runoff pushed the Saco River at Conway above its 9.0 ft flood stage during the day, reaching a crest of approximately 9.6 ft during the evening of May 15 before receding back into its banks overnight. The floodwaters resulted in minor river flooding and shallow inundation of low-lying campgrounds, avoiding structural damage.

On the afternoon of May 15, 2026, minor river flooding occurred along the Pemigewasset River at Plymouth, New Hampshire, driven by basin-wide rainfall averages of 2.75 inches across the Pemigewasset Basin. Water levels rose quickly during the morning, reaching the 13.0-foot flood stage by early afternoon and cresting at approximately 13.1 feet. The brief crest caused minor lowland inundation and shallow water accumulation near Plymouth State University parking areas in Grafton and Belknap Counties before the river fell back below flood stage later that afternoon. No structural damage was reported.

Emergency management reported power outages in Tatum associated with straight-line wind gusts. The time of occurrence and the strength of the wind gust is partially estimated from a Mesonet station recording southwest of town. The cost of damages is also estimated.

A strong thunderstorm brought frequent cloud to ground lightning strikes across Oahu. Some of the lightning struck utility poles which led to power outages for about 35000 customers. The outage areas included, but were not limited to,  Makaha, Aiea, Ewa, Kapolei, Makakilo, Mililani, Pearl City, Waikele, Waimalu and Waipahu. According to HECO, a lightning strike ignited a fire in the switchyard at Kahe Power Plant shortly after 3 p.m., which damaged equipment. Flights at the Daniel K. Inouye International Airport were also delayed due to the lightning.

Heavy rainfall associated with thunderstorms developed over Oahu. This led to flash flooding and multiple roads were closed. Water flooded a residence in Royal Kunia. Flooding was reported on Farrington Highway in Waipahu, Kamehameha Highway near the Waikane Stream, and Waiahole Valley Road.
